Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "GWAS and ExWAS of blood Mitochondrial DNA copy number identifies 71 loci and highlights a potential causal role in dementia" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 3 peer reviewers, including Magnus Nordborg as the Reviewing Editor and Reviewer #1, and the evaluation has been overseen by Y M Dennis Lo as the Senior Editor.

The reviewers have discussed their reviews with one another, and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this to help you prepare a revised submission.

Essential revisions:

1. Your method for estimating mtDNA copy number needs to be better described and explored. We need: a more detailed description of the approach; a more thorough benchmarking (comparing to standard approaches and against estimates from sequencing data); a more thorough description of the phenotype and its distribution; comparisons with age, sex and other UK Biobank phenotypes; description of samples removed and the rationale for removing them.

2. More thorough Mendelian Randomisation analysis: test for pleiotropy using Heidi; perform comparative analysis using all genome wide significant hits (with accompanying discussion of any differing results).

3. Place work in context of other two highly similar recent studies (Longchamps 2021 and Hagg 2021).

4. Data release: code should be on GitHub, raw data for mtDNA-CN estimates and covariates provided where possible, summary statistics uploaded to GWAS catalogue.

5. A bit more discussion of potential population structure confounding? You focus is on individuals of European decent, with meta-analysis including non-Europeans giving similar results.

Reviewer #1:

This is an original human GWAS study that treats mitochondrial copy number variation as a trait, and investigates its genetic basis, as well as its association with (and possible causal role in) various human diseases. The main strength of the study is the development of a method for estimating mitochondrial number from standard array data. This makes it possible to reuse the vast UK Biobank data (n = 383,476) and work with much larger sample sizes than previous studies. The estimated phenotypes are sensibly QC-ed using various data.

They then carry out a standard GWAS, identify 71 significant loci, show that these are significantly over-represented in a priori candidates, and argue convincingly that this could help us understand how mitochondrial copy number is regulated at a cellular level. They show that rare SAMHD1 variants associated with high copy number are also associated with increased cancer risk, and, finally, that mitochondrial copy number may play a role in dementia.

The study represents clever re-use of data, and the findings appear to be well supported and should be interesting to a broad audience. Unlike many human GWAS, there is clearly real biology here.

Your analyses appear admirably solid to me, but this need to be verified by an expert on human GWAS. The same is true for the novelty of the results.

The only improvement I would like to see lies in the description of the estimated phenotype. There is little detail about its distribution, and I would also like to learn more about the factors influencing it, including, obviously, an estimate of much of the variation your 71 loci explain, and a discussion of what explains the rest of the variation. The UK Biobank is full of data…

Reviewer #2:

Mitochondrial DNA copy number is a significant aspect of mitochondrion function, both of which have been linked to disease states. This is an interesting assessment of the genetic basis for variation in mitochondrial DNA copy number. The authors describe a new method for mtDNA CN estimation, although additional benchmarking and validation is warranted in this reviewer's opinion. The GWAS/ExWAS analyses are fairly standard and identify genetic variants likely influencing mtDNA CN. The implementation of the MR analyses is more superficial; it remains unclear in this reviewer's opinion that pleiotropy has been effectively ruled out. The estimates of mtDNA CN and other non-other non-identifiable information (eg, sex, age, ethnic group, etc) necessary to replicate the author's findings should be made publicly available as easily accessible supplementary files.

1. Regarding the method for mtDNA estimation. The method is barely described in the main body of the manuscript. More information should be provided in the main manuscript given that the method it is so essential for this work. Greater clarity about the reproducibility would have helped. Also, it appears that the estimates of mtDNA CN were not tested against a standard with known CN, could this be performed? Some benchmark was done with qPCR estimates, while the results of the methods here developed and qPCR are positively correlated, the magnitude of the correlation is moderate. Finally, wow does the new method compare with sequencing based estimates? All in all, more benchmarking of the method in the main manuscript would greatly improve the paper.

2. Besides better description of the methods for mtDNA CN estimation, a much more detailed description of the mtDNA CN data should be provided in the main manuscript. It is not possible to properly understand/appreciate the reported associations and MR results without such description of the underlying mtDNA CN data.

3. In this reviewer's opinion the pre-computed mtDNA estimates and other non-identifiable information (eg, sex, age, ethnic group, etc) necessary to replicate the author's findings should be made publicly available in supplementary text format files and that could be easily accessible to readers. If the text files are too large for eLife the authors should upload the files to Dryad, dbGaP, etc.

4. The author's state that "After quality control, 359,689 British, 10,598 Irish, 13,189 Other White, 6,172 South Asian, and 6,133 African samples had suitable array-based mtDNA-CN estimates for subsequent GWAS testing. It is unclear what the authors mean by "suitable" in this case. It would also be good to describe in the main text how many were unsuitable in each case and the reasons why these estimates did not match the requirement for suitability.

5. It is unclear if the authors detected ethnic and/or population differences that might confound the other downstream analyses. It is also unclear what are the error and reproducibility of the CN estimates.

6. The influence of sex and age are not described (or superficially described).

7. The presentation of the MR results is unconvincing. For the analysis, the authors have not ruled out pleiotropy in my opinion. Heterogeneity tests such as Heidi should be used Zhu, Z. et al. Integration of summary data from GWAS and eQTL studies predicts complex trait gene targets. Nat. Genet. 48, 481-487 (2016) in addition to MREgger. Also, dementia seems to have the largest error bars around its OR estimates. More detailed analyses and discussion could help here.

Reviewer #3:

This work develops and presents an adapted approach to quantify mitochondrial DNA copy number (mtDNA-CN) from DNA genotyping arrays (named AutoMitoC) by using the intensity of probes emanating from the mitochondrial genome and then using a series of control and normalisation steps that can be applied within a standard framework across data from different populations. They use their estimates of mtDNA-CN as a quantitative trait within a genome wide association study to identify genes and genetic variants that are associated with variation in this phenotype, using both rare and common polymorphisms. Through multiple complementary approaches they then identify a large number of genes that are linked to mtDNA-CN, including those that are involved in mtDNA depletion disorders and various different components of mitochondrial function. Within this, using rare variant analysis they find SAMHD1 as a potential regulator of mtDNA-CN (and possibly breast cancer risk), and the authors suggest that the product of this gene may make a good draggable target to control the downstream effects of altered mtDNA-CN. Finally, the study uses Mendelian Randomisation analyses between genetically determined mtDNA-CN and a selection of disease phenotypes that have been linked to mitochondrial processes previously, and in doing so they find a link between mtDNA-CN and dementia.

In general, the work appears robust and achieves the aims of uncovering the genetic architecture of a disease relevant phenotype, and its potential downstream implications. Readers of this article should be aware of two further studies that have performed similar analyses on largely the same data as those described in this paper. The first by Hagg et al. (2021) considers largely the same set of individuals and identifies 50 genetic loci associated with variation in mtDNA-CN across individuals. The second by Longchamps et al. (2021), finds 129 independent genetic variant associations and includes additional data from a different cohort. The study presented here discusses the findings of Hagg et al. (although a direct comparison of genes is not given) but does not interrogate and compare results from the Longchamps study, which is necessary to truly understand the genetic architecture of this trait and to place this work in context. For the comparison with Hagg et al., the authors suggest that their improved method for mtDNA-CN quantification leads to a higher number of genetic associations, although a more formal comparison of AutoMitoC and standard approaches against control data like that generated from qPCR would make this statement more robust (there is a comparison between AutoMitoC and Hagg et al. quantification in the Discussion section, although it is not clear whether this comparison is like-for-like using the same set of samples). In general, many of the bigger picture biological findings are shared across the three studies (many shared loci and enrichment of genes involved in mtDNA depletion syndrome and mitochondrial processes), which is an excellent advert for reproducible science.

The additional strength of the work by Kong et al. are two extra pieces of analyses not found in other works – an analysis of rare variants and the implementation of Mendelian Randomisation to link variation in mtDNA-CN to disease risk. For the Mendelian Randomisation analyses, authors select genetic variants associated with mtDNA-CN based on their likely role in mitochondrial processes (those variants falling within or close to a mitocarta gene). This is rational given the assumption in Mendelian Randomisation analyses, that genetic instruments should be causal, but it would also be useful to also consider the full set of genetic variants that are associated with mtDNA-CN at genome wide significance to test the relevance of selecting a subset of genetic variants.

1. Page 3, lines 3-8 (but also throughout the text): Whilst it is appreciated that there is a vast body of literature pointing to links between mtDNA-CN and complex disease, I think it is worth briefly discussing caveats to these results in order to properly frame the relevance of the work. For instance, there are many studies showing that links between blood derived mtDNA-CN and age-related diseases may at least in part be driven by cell type composition. There is also plenty of debate around whether mtDNA-CN in blood is indicative of processes in other tissues which might be more relevant for each particular disease. Much of these caveats have been recently neatly summarised in Picard 2021.

2. Page 9, lines 16-17: "We postulated that mtDNA-CN loci may regulate copy number by inducing changes in expression of genes that are directly transcribed from mtDNA.": I don't understand this rationale – are you postulating that lower/higher expression from the MT genome may trigger changes in copy number (and thus these may be modulated by variants influencing expression)? If so, this should be stated more clearly, if not, please explain the thinking here. I also think that it is worth rewording your conclusions from this analysis, as there is no test of directionality.

3. Page 9: lines 31-41: Similar to point 2, it would be good to be a clear rationale for the comparison of loci associated with mtDNA-CN and heteroplasmy level.

4. Page 10: lines 29-35: It would be good to see statistical tests comparing the fractions of genes that fall into the mitochondrial process categories described here, versus proportions of genes in these categories in Mitocarta as a whole – are these categories enriched for genes identified in this study?

5. Page 25: lines 20-31: Links should be provided in any revised manuscript, including the GitHub repository for the method, and summary statistics should be uploaded to the GWAS catalogue.

6. Figures: In general, the figures are not particularly clear and should be improved for publication. For example, axes text is often too small and difficult to read, and text labels on figures 1 and 2 are not aligned properly.

results.result: AutoMitoC is a novel method for array-based mtDNA-CN estimation that incorporates three key methodological innovations: (1) using globally rare variants instead of common variants for autosomal signal normalization, eliminating the need for LD pruning; (2) empirically detecting cross-hybridizing probes through association testing rather than sequence homology; and (3) using PCA instead of median signal intensity to derive the primary MT signal estimate.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C24-C27 describe the AutoMitoC method and its innovations. The methodological improvements are clearly described in the manuscript with supporting figures (Figure 1 and supplements). The rationale for each innovation is provided, and the method is positioned as an improvement over the existing MitoPipeline approach.

results.result: AutoMitoC was validated against complementary mtDNA-CN measurement methods, showing significant correlation with WES-based estimates (r=0.45) and stronger correlation with qPCR-based estimates (r=0.64), with robust performance across multiple ethnic groups (r>0.53). AutoMitoC demonstrated superior concordance with WES compared to the method by Hägg et al., 2021 (r=0.45 vs r=0.33).
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C30, C85, and C97 describe validation results with specific correlation coefficients and p-values. The validation was performed in independent cohorts (UKBiobank subset with WES and INTERSTROKE study with qPCR) and across multiple ethnicities. The statistical evidence is strong (p<2.23×10^-308), and the validation approach is comprehensive. Figure 1 supplements 5-6 provide visual support.

results.result: AutoMitoC was applied to 395,781 UKBiobank participants, revealing expected associations with demographic factors: age (beta=-0.08 SDs per decade; p<2.23×10^-308), sex (females higher by beta=0.12 SDs; p=1.67×10^-299), and ethnicity (South Asians and Africans lower than Europeans by beta=-0.18; p<10^-47). These factors collectively explained 0.83% of mtDNA-CN variance.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C31-C35 report demographic associations that are consistent with prior literature (as stated by authors). The large sample size (N=395,781), highly significant p-values, and consistency with previous reports support these findings. The variance explained is modest but expected for demographic factors. Figure 2A shows the distribution.

results.result: Blood cell composition is strongly associated with mtDNA-CN levels, with neutrophil count being the strongest predictor (beta=-0.31; 9.9% variance explained), followed by white blood cell count (beta=-0.25; 6.3% variance) and platelet count (beta=0.07; 0.5% variance). Collectively, these three cell types explained 12.3% of mtDNA-CN variance.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C42 describe associations between blood cell counts and mtDNA-CN with specific effect sizes, confidence intervals, and variance explained. The findings are well-supported by statistical evidence (p<2.23×10^-308) and are consistent with known confounding by blood cell composition. Figure 2B provides visual support. The identification of neutrophil count as a stronger predictor than the commonly adjusted white blood cell count is a notable finding.

results.result: GWAS of 11,453,766 common variants in 383,476 European participants identified 9,602 genome-wide significant variants, encompassing 82 independent signals in 72 loci. After NUMT sensitivity analysis removing 2 loci, 80 independent signals in 70 loci remained, explaining 1.48% of mtDNA-CN variance. The genomic inflation factor (1.16) and LD score intercept (1.036) indicated polygenicity rather than population stratification.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C43-C51 describe the primary GWAS results with specific numbers of variants, loci, and quality control metrics. The large sample size, appropriate quality control (including NUMT sensitivity analysis), and use of LD score regression to assess inflation support these findings. Figure 3A shows the Manhattan plot. The claim of 71 loci in C3 appears to be a summary combining GWAS (70) and ExWAS (1) results.

results.result: Fine-mapping of the 80 independent GWAS signals revealed that 17 (22%) mapped to a single candidate causal variant, 32 (39%) to ≤5 variants, and 42 (51%) to ≤10 variants. Credible sets for 11 signals overlapped with genes responsible for rare mtDNA depletion disorders (DGUOK, MGME1, TFAM, TWNK, POLG2, TYMP), and 10 of 19 (53%) known mtDNA depletion genes harbored at least suggestive associations (p<5×10^-6).
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C56 describe fine-mapping results using FINEMAP algorithm with specific proportions and gene overlaps. The enrichment of mtDNA depletion genes provides biological validation of the GWAS findings. Figure 3B shows the credible set size distribution. The methodology is appropriate and the results are clearly presented.

results.result: Comparison with previous GWAS studies showed that 41 of 66 (62%) signals from Hägg et al., 2021 were replicated at Bonferroni significance, with 48 (60%) of the present study's 80 signals being novel relative to Hägg et al. For Longchamps et al., 2022, 70 of 116 (60%) detectable variants were replicated at Bonferroni significance, with 11 (14%) of the present study's signals being novel relative to both prior studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C60 describe systematic comparison with two major prior GWAS studies. The authors appropriately note limitations (lack of full summary statistics for reverse lookup) and provide detailed replication statistics. The identification of novel loci is supported by the larger sample size and improved methodology. Supplementary files provide detailed variant-level comparisons.

results.result: Transethnic comparison showed that European GWAS effect estimates were highly correlated with those from South Asian (r=0.97; p=2.2×10^-15) and African (r=0.88; p=9.1×10^-5) ancestry groups, indicating consistency of genetic effects across populations.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C62 report transethnic correlations with strong statistical significance. Figure 3 supplement 3 provides visual support. The high correlations suggest that genetic effects on mtDNA-CN are largely consistent across ancestries, though the smaller sample sizes in non-European groups limit power for independent discovery.

results.result: Integration with mt-eQTL and heteroplasmy GWAS data revealed that nonsynonymous variants in LONP1 and TBRG4, and an intronic variant in MRPS35, were associated with MT gene expression changes. Four heteroplasmy loci (TINCR/LONP1, TWNK/MPRL43, TFAM, PRKAB1) were also associated with mtDNA-CN at genome-wide significance with concordant directionality.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C64 describe integration with external datasets (Ali et al., 2019 for mt-eQTL; Nandakumar et al., 2021 for heteroplasmy). The overlap provides biological insight into mechanisms, though the authors appropriately note that directionality of causation cannot be definitively established. The concordant directionality for heteroplasmy loci strengthens the findings.

results.result: Gene prioritization using DEPICT identified 91 genes (FDR p<0.05), with GeneMANIA discovering an additional 20 related genes. Among 107 total prioritized genes, MT functions were significantly enriched (mitochondrion organization, MT nucleoid, MT genome maintenance, MT matrix; all FDR p<0.001). Twenty-seven genes (25%) encoded MT-localized proteins (4.2-fold enrichment; p=1.0×10^-10), with 16 (57%) belonging to the 'Mitochondrial central dogma' pathway (threefold enrichment; p=1.3×10^-5). Prioritized genes showed higher PGC-1A-induced fold change than all MT genes (p=0.04).
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C70 describe comprehensive pathway and gene ontology analyses using established methods (DEPICT, GeneMANIA, MitoCarta3). The enrichment statistics are significant and biologically coherent, pointing to specific MT processes. Figure 3C-D provides visual support. The PGC-1A enrichment (C69) has a marginal p-value (0.04) but is consistent with the overall pattern.

results.result: ExWAS of 18,890 genes in 147,740 participants identified SAMHD1 as the only gene reaching exome-wide significance, with carriers of rare mutations (prevalence 0.75%) having higher mtDNA-CN (beta=0.23 SDs; p=2.6×10^-19). TFAM showed suggestive association (beta=-0.33; p=4.2×10^-6). Rare variants in SAMHD1 and TFAM accounted for 0.06% of mtDNA-CN variance; combined with common loci, total genetic variance explained was 1.55%.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C75, C4, and C73 describe ExWAS results with appropriate statistical thresholds (exome-wide significance p<2.65×10^-6). The SAMHD1 finding is highly significant and biologically plausible given its role in dNTP metabolism. Figure 4A shows the QQ plot. The modest variance explained by rare variants (0.06%) is expected given their low frequency.

results.result: Phenome-wide association testing of SAMHD1 mutation carrier status (99.4% heterozygotes) revealed approximately twofold increased risk of breast cancer (OR=1.91; p=2.7×10^-8) and increased risk of 'cancer (suspected or other)' (OR=1.52; p=1.1×10^-6). The association with mtDNA-CN remained significant after excluding cancer patients (beta=0.26; p=7.8×10^-15), indicating the effect is not driven by cancer status.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C76-C78, and C89 describe PheWAS results with phenome-wide significant associations. The sensitivity analysis excluding cancer patients (C78) strengthens the interpretation that SAMHD1 mutations affect mtDNA-CN independently of cancer status. Figure 4B shows the Manhattan plot. The finding is biologically plausible given SAMHD1's role in DNA repair and tumor suppression.

results.result: Mendelian randomization analysis using 27 genetic variants near MT protein-encoding genes showed that low mtDNA-CN has a causal effect on dementia risk (OR=1.94 per 1 SD decrease; p=7.5×10^-4). Sensitivity analyses showed no evidence of pleiotropy (MR-PRESSO p=0.51; Egger intercept p=0.47), and Steiger directionality test supported causation from mtDNA-CN to dementia (p=1.9×10^-62). The association was replicated in an independent dataset (OR=1.41; p=0.04993).
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C79-C83, and C92 describe Mendelian randomization results with appropriate sensitivity analyses. The use of multiple MR methods, pleiotropy tests, directionality assessment, and independent replication strengthen causal inference. However, the replication p-value (0.04993) is barely significant, and the wide confidence intervals reflect limited power. Figure 6 shows the results. The authors appropriately acknowledge this as the first MR evidence for this relationship.

results.result: The genetic findings indicate that mtDNA-CN is a complex biomarker under substantial nuclear genetic regulation, reflecting specific MT processes related to dNTP metabolism and mtDNA replication, maintenance, and organization. These processes are causally related to human diseases, particularly dementia.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C8, C86, and C100-C102 represent the authors' overall conclusions drawn from the genetic analyses. These conclusions are well-supported by the convergent evidence from GWAS, ExWAS, pathway analyses, and Mendelian randomization. The enrichment of mtDNA depletion genes, MT central dogma pathway, and the causal association with dementia provide strong support for these interpretations.

results.result: SAMHD1 is a multifaceted enzyme involved in tumor suppression and dNTP metabolism. Rare homozygous/compound heterozygous loss-of-function mutations cause Aicardi Goutieres' syndrome, while approximately 1 in 130 UKBiobank participants carry heterozygous mutations conferring twofold breast cancer risk. Previous work (Franzolin et al., 2015) showed that siRNA knockdown of SAMHD1 partially recovered mtDNA-CN in DGUOK-mutant fibroblasts.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C88, C90-C91 describe prior knowledge about SAMHD1 supported by citations. The calculation in C90 (1 in 130 = 0.75% carrier prevalence) is correct. These claims provide important biological context for interpreting the novel findings about SAMHD1 and mtDNA-CN.

results.result: Prior studies support the relationship between mtDNA-CN and dementia: Silzer et al., 2019 (N=46) found lower blood mtDNA-CN in cognitive impairment; Andrews and Goate, 2020 (N=1,025) found brain mtDNA-CN associated with cognitive measures (beta=-4.02 for MMSE; p=1.07×10^-7); Yang et al., 2021 found associations with incident neurodegenerative disease. Combined with the present MR findings, mtDNA-CN represents both a marker and mediator of dementia.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C96 summarize prior literature with appropriate citations and integrate it with the present findings. The conclusion in C96 is reasonable given the convergent evidence from observational studies and the present MR analysis, though the authors appropriately note that further work is needed to determine which specific MT processes mediate dementia pathogenesis.

results.result: The present study represents the most comprehensive genetic assessment of mtDNA-CN published to date, identifying 48 (60%) novel loci relative to Hägg et al., 2021 and 11 (14%) novel loci not reported in either Hägg et al., 2021 or Longchamps et al., 2022.
results.evaluation: Claims C84, C58, and C60 assert the comprehensiveness and novelty of the study. This is supported by the larger sample size (~100,000 more participants than Hägg et al.), improved methodology (AutoMitoC), inclusion of ExWAS, and systematic comparison showing substantial novel discovery. The claim is justified.

results.result: The study has limitations including: (1) Mendelian randomization analyses were underpowered for broad disease survey, with large confidence intervals even for dementia; (2) whole blood mtDNA-CN reflects heterogeneous cell populations, and unmeasured cell subpopulations may confound results despite adjustment for major cell types.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C99 describe limitations acknowledged by the authors. These are valid concerns: the wide CI for dementia MR (1.55-2.32) reflects limited power, and blood cell heterogeneity is a known confounder of mtDNA-CN measurements. The authors appropriately acknowledge these limitations.

results.result: Background claims establish that: mitochondria are semiautonomous organelles executing fundamental cellular processes; MT dysfunction has been implicated in human disorders; mtDNA-CN is a blood-based marker of MT DNA abundance; observational studies link lower mtDNA-CN to age-related diseases and higher mtDNA-CN to cancer; mtDNA depletion syndromes involve 60-80% drops in mtDNA-CN due to defects in 19 known genes; ~50 common loci have been identified; blood mtDNA-CN is confounded by cell composition and correlates poorly with other tissues.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C23 provide background information supported by citations to prior literature. These establish the scientific context and rationale for the study. The claims are appropriately cited and represent established knowledge in the field.
